title: Raises & Promotions
description: Raise math, rising prices, and how to ask for more.
wolfLine: Nobody hands the meat to the wolf who waits by the door.

inflation.definition: Prices rising over time, so the same money buys a little less each year.
inflation.example: Groceries that cost $400 cost $420 after 5% inflation.

cost-of-living-adjustment.definition: A raise meant to keep up with rising prices, not to reward performance. Often called a COLA.
cost-of-living-adjustment.example: Everyone gets 3% in January because prices rose 3%.

merit-raise.definition: A raise that rewards how well you did your job.
merit-raise.example: A 5% raise for beating your targets, when the average was 3%.

performance-review.definition: A regular meeting, often yearly, where your manager rates your work. Raises are often decided there.
performance-review.example: Your December review: “exceeds expectations,” plus a 5% raise.

steps.context: Raises are usually a percent. To get the new pay, multiply by 1 plus the percent: a 4% raise is × 1.04.
steps.prompt: $50,000 with a 4% raise. What’s the new salary?
$20 an hour with a 5% raise. What’s the new rate?
From $40,000 to $42,000. What percent raise is that?
A 3% raise on $48,000 adds how much per year?
Paid every two weeks, how much more is that per paycheck, before deductions?
A 3% raise on $60,000 is bigger in dollars than a 4% raise on $40,000.

lessons.title: Raises vs. Rising Prices
lessons.summary: A raise only counts if it beats rising prices.

steps.context: [[Inflation]] is prices rising over time. If prices rise 3% a year, the same groceries cost 3% more next year.
steps.prompt: Prices rose 3% this year. Your raise was 3%. Can you buy more than last year?
steps.explain: Your pay and your prices moved together.

steps.prompt: Your raise was 2% and prices rose 4%. What happened to your buying power?
steps.explain: Your pay went up less than your costs.

steps.prompt: A real raise is roughly your raise minus inflation. 5% raise, 3% inflation?
steps.explain: 5% − 3% = about 2% more buying power.

steps.context: A [[cost-of-living adjustment]] (COLA) is a raise meant to keep up with rising prices, not to reward you.
steps.prompt: Your company gives everyone 3% to match rising prices. What is it?
steps.explain: It keeps you level. It’s not a reward.

steps.prompt: A raise that only matches inflation leaves you no richer.
steps.explain: Same buying power as before.

steps.prompt: Groceries cost $400 a month. Prices rise 5%. What’s the new monthly cost?

lessons.title: Kinds of Raises
lessons.summary: Merit, cost-of-living and promotion: what each one means.

steps.context: A [[merit raise]] rewards how well you did. It’s often decided at your [[performance review]], a regular meeting about your work.
steps.prompt: What decides a merit raise?
choices: How well you did your job
steps.explain: Performance, not the calendar.

steps.prompt: What kind of raise is it?
items: A bigger raise for top performers
New title, new duties, new pay
A reward for beating your sales goals
Moving from cashier to shift lead

steps.prompt: Which usually brings the biggest jump in pay?
steps.explain: New role, new pay band.

steps.prompt: Switching jobs can bring a bigger raise than staying put.
steps.explain: Job changers often get bigger jumps, though it’s never guaranteed.

steps.prompt: Promoted from $46,000 to $53,000. What percent raise is that? Round to the nearest whole percent.
Your review says “meets expectations” and you get 2%. Prices rose 3%. Best response?
choices: Ask what it takes to earn more next time, and track it
steps.explain: Turn a weak raise into a plan.

lessons.title: Asking for a Raise
lessons.summary: Raises go to people who ask, with proof.

steps.title: Build your case
steps.body: Raises usually go to people who ask, and back it up. Keep a running list of wins: problems solved, money saved, praise from customers. Then look up what your role pays elsewhere.

steps.prompt: Put asking for a raise in order.
items: Collect your wins and pay research
Ask your manager for a meeting
Make your case with a specific number
Agree on next steps and a date
steps.explain: Prepare, ask, propose, follow up.

steps.prompt: When’s the best time to ask?
choices: A few weeks before budgets or reviews are set
The day after a big mistake
steps.explain: Ask while the money is still being divided up.

steps.prompt: What’s the strongest reason for a raise?
choices: What you’ve achieved, and what the role pays elsewhere
why: True, but it’s your problem, not their reason to pay more.
Risky, and it makes it about someone else.
steps.explain: Your value to them is the argument that works.

steps.prompt: If the answer is no, it’s fine to ask what would make it a yes later.
steps.explain: Get the goals in writing.

steps.prompt: You ask for 8% on $45,000. What number do you say?

lessons.title: Review Day
lessons.summary: Your manager offers a number. What do you say?

steps.prompt: Your manager offers 3%. Your research says the role pays 10% more elsewhere. Best response?
choices: Thank them, share your research, and ask if 6% is possible
why: You leave money on the table without even asking.
Only threaten what you’re ready to do.
steps.explain: Calm, specific and backed by numbers.

steps.prompt: They say the budget is frozen until summer. Next move?
choices: Ask to revisit it in summer, in writing
steps.explain: A date in writing is a promise you can come back to.

steps.prompt: They offer a better title but no raise. What do you ask?
choices: When the pay for that title will follow
steps.explain: Titles are nice. Pay is nicer.

steps.prompt: Getting your goals agreed in writing makes the next raise conversation easier.
steps.explain: Hit the goals, point to the email.

steps.prompt: You negotiate from 3% to 5% on $50,000. How much more per year is that?
Your raise comes through. First thought?
choices: Give the extra money a job before it disappears
steps.explain: That’s the last lesson in this unit.

lessons.title: Raises Stack Up
lessons.summary: Every raise builds on the last one.

steps.context: Raises build on each other: next year’s raise is a percent of this year’s bigger pay.
steps.prompt: $40,000 with a 5% raise this year and 5% again next year. What’s the pay after two years?
Compare: two raises of $2,000 each. Pay after two years?
Why is the percent version a bit higher?
choices: The second raise is 5% of a bigger number

steps.prompt: Starting at $48,000 vs. $45,000, both with a 3% raise. How far apart are they after one year?
steps.explain: $49,440 − $46,350 = $3,090. The gap grows with every raise.

steps.prompt: Your starting salary matters because every future raise builds on it.
steps.explain: That’s why negotiating it is worth it.

steps.prompt: Which helps most over a career?
choices: Higher starting pay plus regular raises
steps.explain: Growth on top of a good base.

lessons.title: Ty’s Promotion
lessons.summary: A bigger number can hide a smaller hourly rate.

story.title: Promotion or pay cut?
story.body:
Ty earns **$17.50** an hour and works about **38** hours a week.

The store offers Ty a promotion to shift lead: a salary of **$41,000** a year. The catch: shift leads work about **45** hours a week, and as a salaried manager Ty wouldn’t get overtime.

steps.prompt: What does Ty earn now in a year? $17.50 × 38 hours × 52 weeks.
How much more a year is the salaried offer?
At 45 hours a week, how many hours a year is the new job?
What does the new job pay per hour? $41,000 ÷ 2,340, rounded to the cent.
So is it a raise per hour?
choices: Barely: 2 cents more an hour, for 7 more hours a week
steps.explain: More money, but almost all of it is from working more.

steps.prompt: What could make the promotion worth it anyway?
choices: The title and experience lead to bigger raises later
steps.explain: Sometimes the next step pays off at the step after.

lessons.title: Give Your Raise a Job
lessons.summary: Catch the raise before lifestyle creep does.

steps.context: When pay goes up, spending tends to drift up too. That’s [[lifestyle creep]], and it eats raises.
steps.prompt: Your take-home rose $200 a month. Six months later you have no more saved. What happened?
steps.explain: The extra money quietly turned into extra spending.

steps.prompt: What’s a simple rule many people use for raises?
choices: Save at least half of every raise
steps.explain: Half for future you, half to enjoy.

steps.prompt: Your take-home went up $300 a month. Plan it: at least half goes to savings and goals.
steps.explain: Savings got at least $150 and every dollar has a job.

steps.prompt: Saving $150 a month from a raise for a year adds up to?
Raising your 401(k) contribution by 1% with each raise is an easy habit.
steps.explain: You never miss money you never got used to.

steps.prompt: Raise day: put it in order.
steps.explain: Know it, save it, plan it, enjoy it.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Raises & Promotions
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: $52,000 with a 3% raise. What’s the new salary?
Your raise was 3% and prices rose 4%. Your buying power…
steps.explain: Prices beat your raise.

steps.prompt: A promotion usually brings a bigger jump than a cost-of-living adjustment.
steps.explain: New role, new pay band.

steps.prompt: From $30.00 to $31.50 an hour. What percent raise is that?
